conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 18, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Adding Braggtown and Merrick-Moore to the Longtime Homeowner Grant Program (Item 26)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 2-5 on DeDreana Freeman's amendment to immediately include Braggtown and Merrick-Moore in the city's tax-relief pilot alongside Walltown before unanimously approving Walltown alone.
conflicts.side_a_position: Immediately expand the city's Longtime Homeowner Grant criteria to add Braggtown and Merrick-Moore for the 2019-2020 tax years.
side_a_arguments: Legacy Black homeowners in Braggtown and Merrick-Moore are facing urgent tax-bill spikes and gentrification displacement, and the countywide program only begins with 2021 taxes.
If Council can allocate $79,000 for its own raises, it should extend equivalent relief to long-time homeowners fighting to stay housed.
conflicts.side_b_position: Restrict the city pilot to Walltown based on documented city affordable housing investments while pressing Durham County to expand the countywide relief program to 60% AMI.
side_b_arguments: City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg advised that granting neighborhood tax relief where the city had not made qualifying affordable housing investments creates serious North Carolina constitutional emoluments risk.
A countywide program administered with Durham County at 60% AMI is legally sound and covers all underserved neighborhoods equitably without a patchwork city carve-out.
conflicts.resolution: Amendment Failed 2-5; original Walltown & 2020 tax-year motion subsequently Passed 7-0

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Sept. 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 1051 Olive Branch Road Annexation, Suburban Growth in Southeast Durham, and Post-Planning Commission Revisions
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 on annexing and rezoning 1051 Olive Branch Road for 284 units after the developer revised environmental and cemetery proffers following a June 21 continuance and an April 1-11 Planning Commission denial recommendation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation and rezoning because post-continuance commitments substantially improved environmental protection, resolved gravesite family outreach, and added needed housing supply.
side_a_arguments: Majority members noted that post-June revisions secured 13 of 13 descendant family consents alongside an archaeological study, raised distributed tree save to 24% and open space to 35%, and eliminated three vehicular stream crossings.
Supporters cited Durham's housing supply shortage and contiguous alignment with the previously approved adjacent 1101 Olive Branch Road project.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the suburban annexation and rezoning due to sprawling Southeast Durham growth, cumulative neighborhood impacts, and repeated developer bypassing of the Planning Commission.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (01:00:16) and DeDreana Freeman (01:04:45) maintained their opposition to continued far-flung suburban annexations in the Olive Branch corridor and criticized the cumulative infrastructure and community-cost burden.
Members across Council also raised frustration that developers wait until City Council hearings—bypassing the Planning Commission—to introduce major design concessions.
conflicts.resolution: Council approved annexation and rezoning 5-2 (Freeman and Reece nay) and subsequently approved the statutory Consistency Statement 7-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Courtyards at Doc Nichols Annexation & Rezoning — Low-Density Suburban Growth vs. Accessible Housing & Solar Proffers (Item 16)
conflicts.summary: With Charlie Reece absent, City Council deadlocked 3-3 on Epcon Communities' 133-unit accessible housing proposal in Southeast Durham, defeating the project.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 75-acre annexation and rezoning based on accessible aging-in-place housing, environmental proffers, and $120,000 affordable housing contribution.
side_a_arguments: Provided Durham's first-ever solar conduit residential proffer, 33% tree preservation, and $120,000 dedicated to the city's affordable housing fund.

Middleton and Freelon noted the single-story zero-step courtyard model serves seniors and disability needs in an underserved area, and rejected applying the un-adopted draft Southeast Focus Area Plan against a compliant application.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning as incompatible low-density greenfield sprawl with watershed/stream crossing impacts and luxury price points.
side_b_arguments: At 1.8 units/acre and $500,000-$550,000 home prices, the suburban layout conflicts with smart-growth transit/infrastructure efficiency and the emerging Southeast planning vision.
The Planning Commission recommended denial unanimously (0-12), citing environmental impacts of the stream crossing, buffer encroachment, and neighborhood road safety concerns.
conflicts.resolution: Failed 3-3 on tie vote

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 1, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Latta Park Rezoning — Commercial Expansion, Latta Road Traffic & Eno Watershed Impacts vs. On-Site Affordable Townhomes & Intersection Fixes
conflicts.summary: Latta Park split the Council 6-1 after residents and conservation advocates argued that adding 55,000 sq ft of retail and 200 townhomes at Guess and Latta Roads violated Comprehensive Plan commercial siting, threatened Eno River water quality, and overloaded two-lane Latta Road, while the six-member majority praised unprecedented proffers including 10 60%-AMI townhomes and dual turn lanes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the mixed-use CG(D)/PDR 9.906 rezoning as a needed supply of moderate/affordable townhomes and northern Durham neighborhood retail.
side_a_arguments: Developer proffered over 50 commitments including 10 permanently affordable townhomes at 60% AMI ($1.25M subsidy), 40kW solar, a 1.3-acre park, and 100-year residential stormwater detention.

Dual left-turn lanes improve peak morning Guess/Latta intersection level-of-service from D to C where no NCDOT upgrades are funded, and rejection leaves RS-20 $500k+ McMansions as the by-right alternative.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose commercial and high-density rezoning due to traffic bottlenecks on un-widenable Latta Road, stormwater/Eno watershed risks, and lack of transit walkability.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman voted No after extensive opposition testimony citing level-of-service D egress on Latta Road, right-in/right-out U-turns on Guess Road, and Easley Elementary traffic hazards.
Opponents including Megan Gray and Eno River Association ED Jessica Sheffield noted nearby vacant commercial space, no bus service, and impervious surface runoff above West Point on the Eno.
conflicts.resolution: Council adopted both the Latta Park zoning ordinance and consistency statement by 6-1 roll-call votes, with DeDreana Freeman in dissent.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 1, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Sufficiency of Griffin Place Community Benefits, Affordable Housing Proffer, and Product Integration
conflicts.summary: Council paused the 462-unit Griffin Place annexation and rezoning in eastern Durham because members found initial housing-fund payments, perimeter buffers, and segregated single-family/townhome layouts insufficient relative to the project's scale and state-road congestion.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold the public hearing open until January 3, 2022 to extract stronger affordable housing contributions, better industrial/residential buffering, block-length limits, and improved traffic clarity.
side_a_arguments: Even after raising the affordable housing fund proffer from $150 to $500/unit during the hearing, Council noted the ~$115M project needed stronger design commitments, less rigid product segregation, and better buffering adjacent to Scannell industrial land.
State roads around Cheek and Ferrell Roads lack funded DOT widening, raising urgency around community benefits.
conflicts.side_b_position: Recognize already-proffered traffic signals, 100-year ponds, and Glenn Elementary pedestrian crossings while negotiating additional terms.
side_b_arguments: Applicant argued residential zoning cut trips vs. current industrial zoning and committed to three traffic signals and a $34,000 DPS school contribution.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 7-0 to continue the Griffin Place public hearing open until January 3, 2022.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 18, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: City Council Salary Adjustments During Pandemic Budget Cycle (Item 24)
conflicts.summary: Six Council members voted to raise Council salaries to Durham's $35,200 livable-wage floor starting January 1, 2022 to open officeholding to working-class residents, while DeDreana Freeman dissented over optics and equity toward city employees whose step raises had been paused.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adjust Council member salaries to the city's full-time minimum livable wage ($35,200) and Mayor's salary to $40,536 effective January 1, 2022.
side_a_arguments: Council service requires full-time commitment and dozens of board obligations; sub-living stipends exclude working-class residents and low-wealth candidates.

Outgoing members (including Freelon and Schewel) argued it is an institutional equity reform comparable to recent adjustments in Charlotte and Raleigh, and the City Attorney advised Council cannot bind future budget cycles without passing it now.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose raising Council salaries at this time and prioritize restoring skipped pay steps for municipal workers and resident COVID relief.
side_b_arguments: City staff missed step raises during the pandemic and Council should focus budget dollars on city employees and residents facing hardship first.
Raising post-election stipends alone does not overcome structural fundraising and campaign barriers that prevent working-class candidates from running.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 6-1

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 23, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: City Council Salary Adjustments and Pandemic Budget Priorities (Item 3)
conflicts.summary: A Council majority endorsed raising Council stipends to Durham's livable-wage floor ($35,200 Council / ~$42,000 Mayor) to make officeholding accessible to working-class residents, while DeDreana Freeman opposed moving ahead while employee pay steps had been skipped and Charlie Reece remained torn over spending $78,000.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance an ordinance aligning Council salaries with Durham's full-time minimum livable wage, subject to a public hearing.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon, Jillian Johnson, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Steve Schewel argued sub-living stipends lock working people out of devoting full-time hours to Council service.
Both Charlotte and Raleigh have adopted comparable compensation updates, and City Attorney/Budget staff confirmed Council cannot defer binding a future budget year.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose or question advancing Council raises during pandemic hardship when staff pay steps were skipped and residents need direct relief.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman argued Council should focus first on restoring skipped employee step raises and doubted stipends would overcome campaign cost barriers.
Charlie Reece questioned whether $78,000 was the best pandemic budget choice while Jacqueline Wagstaff urged taxpayer control rather than moving from a part-time stipend model.
conflicts.resolution: Consensus thumbs-up to schedule a public hearing before taking a formal vote

conflicts.meeting_title: Regular Durham City Council Meeting Aug 16, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Courtyards at Southpoint 2 Buffer Protections, ATT Connectivity, and Residential Accountability (Item 18)
conflicts.summary: Residents along Herndon Road and Fenwick Parkway objected to density, stormwater runoff, traffic, and loss of trees along the American Tobacco Trail, prompting Council to press Epcon Southpoint LLC into binding mid-hearing proffers before voting unanimously.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve only with binding written proffers guaranteeing American Tobacco Trail connections, undisturbed buffer trees, traffic calming, and affordable housing support.
side_a_arguments: Neighbors Karen Francola, Dr. Eugene Granger, Barbara Taylor, Bansari Patel, and Trisha Smarr raised flooding, buffer clearing, and Herndon/Fenwick traffic concerns.

Council members pushed Epcon Southpoint LLC to add concrete written commitments for two ATT trail tie-ins, an undisturbed 20-ft ATT buffer outside tie-in corridors, Phase 2 traffic calming, and a $40,000 affordable housing contribution.
conflicts.side_b_position: Initial developer submission relied on standard UDO compliance and a single trail tie-in without Phase 2 traffic-calming or undisturbed-buffer commitments.
side_b_arguments: Applicant attorneys initially defended standard site-plan review for stormwater and buffer management before agreeing to expand written commitments during the hearing.
conflicts.resolution: Epcon Southpoint LLC committed to the added proffers on the record (01:56:10), resolving Council concerns and yielding unanimous 7-0 approval.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 1051 Olive Branch Road Environmental Protections, Grave Relocation, and Suburban Housing Supply (Item 43)
conflicts.summary: Council held a prolonged debate over Pulte Home Company LLC's 284-unit annexation at 1051 Olive Branch Road, pitting housing-supply concerns against East Durham Open Space Plan incompatibility, mass grading, peripheral tree save, and relocation of an on-site cemetery, resulting in continuance to September 7.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue the hearing to seek stronger tree preservation, environmental mitigation, and cemetery/community commitments without immediately killing needed housing stock.
side_a_arguments: Javiera Caballero (02:49:21) and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson (03:08:56) stressed Durham's worsening housing shortage while agreeing existing open questions justified a continuance.

Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:13:19) argued $230k-$300k housing expands supply for working-class firefighters, teachers, and officers while still expressing concern over the gravesite and the negligible 21%-to-22% tree-save increase.

Mayor Steve Schewel (03:04:54) backed increasing supply in Southeast Durham but warned he would vote no immediately given the 'not compatible with East Durham Open Space Plan' staff finding and environmental sensitivity.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose or demand deep substantive redesigns addressing far-flung Southeast Durham sprawl, cost-burden spillover, climate/mass-grading harm, and cemetery removal.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (02:57:53) questioned whether townhouses in far-east Durham near Morrisville actually curb gentrification in Braggtown or Walltown and argued annexation conferred no net benefit to Durham.

DeDreana Freeman (02:23:07, 03:10:27) highlighted cumulative impacts across nine area rezonings, carbon footprint without transit, nearby cost-burdened neighborhoods, and distress over moving a historic cemetery—noting she only supported a continuance if meaningful tree-save and stream-crossing changes returned.
conflicts.resolution: With applicant Tim Sivers' agreement (03:23:52), Council left the public hearing open and continued Item 43 to September 7, 2021.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Duke School $10M Tax-Exempt Revenue Bond Host-Approval Resolution (Item 45)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to pass the federal TEFRA resolution for private Duke School's revenue bonds, with Javiera Caballero voting Nay and Mark-Anthony Middleton raising equity concerns about private tuition and public-service reliance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the routine ministerial TEFRA resolution because the City of Durham incurs zero debt, financial obligation, or taxpayer liability.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:41:30), Pierce Freelon (03:39:47), DeDreana Freeman (03:42:27), and Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:42:00) agreed that federal tax-law pass-through approval carries no city financial risk, though Middleton pressed Duke School officials on $20k-$23k tuition, lack of free/reduced lunch or busing, and reliance on city police/fire.
conflicts.side_b_position: Decline to lend City host-jurisdiction TEFRA approval to a private school revenue bond issuance.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero cast the sole Nay vote on roll call (03:43:18) without stating floor remarks.
conflicts.resolution: TEFRA resolution passed 6-1.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 'We Are The Ones' Violence Prevention Funding Amount, Fund Source, and Scope (Mini-Grants vs. Mutual Aid/Centers)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over how much extra money to allocate from fund balance—versus ARPA—and whether funding should be restricted strictly to mini-grants.
conflicts.side_a_position: Provide an extra $187,600 from fund balance to bring 'We Are The Ones' mini-grants to $250,000 total immediately in FY22.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Charlie Reece, and Mark-Anthony Middleton supported reaching $250,000 immediately to empower grassroots violence-prevention mini-grants rather than deferring to uncertain ARPA scoring.

Restricting the $250,000 allocation to mini-grants addressed concerns from Budget Director Bertha Johnson and Javiera Caballero regarding ARPA procurement and unvetted mutual-aid or center line items.
conflicts.side_b_position: Limit extra one-time fund-balance dollars to $100,000 rather than $187,600 and scrutinize program design before committing $250,000.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel favored adding $100,000 rather than $187,600 to reach $250,000 and cast the sole Nay vote when the $187,600 mini-grant motion was called.
conflicts.resolution: Council passed the $187,600 mini-grant allocation 6-1, with Steve Schewel dissenting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 9, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: City Funding of Weekly COVID-19 Testing (Item 25 CVS Health Contract) vs. Vaccine Mandate or Employee-Paid Testing
conflicts.summary: Council divided sharply over City Manager Wanda Page's proposed $69,700/week CVS Health contract to fund weekly testing for unvaccinated employees out of the self-insured Health Insurance Fund, ultimately pulling the item before a formal vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Do not spend taxpayer or shared employee Health Insurance Fund dollars to subsidize ongoing weekly testing for unvaccinated staff; move toward a vaccine mandate or higher health premiums/employee-paid testing.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel (01:14:19, 02:02:35) argued that paying nearly $70,000/week unfairly shifts costs onto taxpayers and vaccinated employees, urging either a vaccine mandate or requiring unvaccinated workers to pay for testing or higher premiums.
Charlie Reece (via email read at 02:08:53) opposed subsidizing weekly testing and favored a vaccine mandate with medical/religious exemptions and higher premiums for unvaccinated staff.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain a measured transition toward vaccination while addressing UE150 labor concerns, work-hours testing access, attrition risks, and EBO/diversity standards before imposing punitive penalties or mandates.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (01:19:41, 02:10:48), Jillian Johnson (01:47:01, 02:05:02), Javiera Caballero (01:28:16, 02:05:48), and Pierce Freelon (01:34:38, 02:06:55) questioned attrition impacts (with HR staff Anna Davis citing 3% at Houston Methodist and 2% at UVA), testing on work hours, UE150 union proposals, and delay options to examine premium recoupment or vaccine mandates.
Donald Hughes (01:43:41) urged Council not to waive Equal Business Opportunity diversity goals on the testing contract.
conflicts.resolution: By consensus (02:14:26-02:19:43), Item 25 was held off the regular meeting agenda, and City Manager Wanda Page agreed to cancel the October 18 testing start and return with data and revised options for a vaccine mandate or premium adjustments.

conflicts.meeting_title: Regular Durham City Council Meeting Aug 16, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Junction & Ferrell Road 222-Acre Industrial Annexation Timing and Neighborhood Impacts (Item 19)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-1 on annexing 222 acres for speculative light-industrial warehousing along Junction and Ferrell Roads, balancing urgent industrial land supply against premature infrastructure and community-equity concerns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation to unlock a premier industrial site ranked 14/14 in Durham's Industrial Land Study and generate tax base and industrial jobs.
side_a_arguments: Majority members noted the scarcity of ready industrial land in Durham and highlighted regional economic-development support from NCRR and the Durham Chamber of Commerce.
County Industrial Light zoning already existed by right, so city annexation ensured municipal utility service, tax revenue, and direct zoning translation.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose premature 222-acre annexation without an identified end-user, committed infrastructure readiness, or protection for long-time nearby homeowners facing tax pressure.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman (03:06:23) opposed annexing 222 acres without confirmed tenants or full infrastructure and argued that industrial growth without parallel tax-relief tools burdens longtime neighboring residents.
Neighbors Bonita Green and Jason Bazdula raised local traffic, quality-of-life, and impact concerns.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and UEA passed 5-1 with DeDreana Freeman dissenting (Charlie Reece absent), followed by approval of direct translational zoning.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Longtime Homeowner Grant Program Expansion: Citywide vs. Targeted Equity and Staff Capacity
conflicts.summary: Following Charlie Reece's proposal to hold applications open and rapidly craft a temporary citywide homeowner tax-relief program ahead of the joint City-County program, Council debated equity targeting, included neighborhoods (Braggtown, Merrick-Moore, Walltown), and Community Development staffing capacity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Create a temporary citywide property-tax relief program for the 2020-21 gap year to ensure all burdened longtime low-income homeowners qualify legally and equitably until the joint County program improves.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (04:11:36, 04:18:09, 04:32:16) argued citywide investments city-wide justify legal defensibility whereas ad-hoc neighborhood additions face legal hurdles cited by Assistant City Attorney Krista Kucera, offering to sunset the city program once the County raises AMI limits and benefit caps.
DeDreana Freeman (04:16:52, 04:27:11, 04:50:24) prioritized immediate gap-year relief so Braggtown, Merrick-Moore, and Walltown residents are not left out of 2019-2020 tax cycles.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the 2019 cycle under current parameters through August 31 and avoid a rushed citywide expansion without staff capacity, cost modeling, and equity targeting.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (04:23:20, 04:41:41, 04:51:47) argued against blanket 'equality' floodgates in affluent areas in favor of targeted 'equity' investments (sidewalks, safety, targeted relief) in historically disinvested neighborhoods, citing Reginald Johnson's staffing constraints.

Jillian Johnson (04:28:51, 04:35:56), Pierce Freelon (04:45:52), and Steve Schewel (04:37:30, 04:48:50) respected staff capacity warnings (vacancies from retirement and medical leave) and supported letting the current program finish through Aug. 31 while directing staff to return in early August with a scoping and resource plan-to-make-a-plan.
conflicts.resolution: Council reached consensus thumbs-up (04:53:00-04:53:17) allowing staff to extend current applications administratively to August 31 and bring an assessment/scoping timeline for gap-year options to the first August work session.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 21, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Preserving Wheels Fun Park Roller Skating Rink vs. Full Aquatics Site Redevelopment (Item 18)
conflicts.summary: Council members split over how the Ratio States NC aquatics study at Wheels Fun Park should treat the existing indoor roller skating rink, with three members drawing a hard red line to preserve the rink while two others urged waiting for broad community survey input.
conflicts.side_a_position: Explicitly rule out demolishing the roller skating rink and prioritize preserving an affordable Black and community skating institution alongside aquatics improvements.
side_a_arguments: Wheels' roller skating rink is a uniquely important, beloved recreation institution for Durham families and youth of color that should not be put on the chopping block.
Community advocates, including speaker Ideal Ortiz, warned against sacrificing the only local indoor roller rink without clear guarantees.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid prejudging design scenarios before conducting an open community survey on both public aquatics needs and the rink.
side_b_arguments: Durham faces a severe shortage of public swimming pool capacity, and early engineering/community feedback should evaluate all site configurations openly.
Restricting consultant study options prematurely could limit viable ways to meet citywide aquatics equity goals.
conflicts.resolution: Informational / Placed on Consent Agenda (staff instructed to convey Council's feedback on preserving skating alongside robust public engagement)

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Durham County Transit Plan Priorities: Bus Service Equity, Commuter Rail Costs, and City Governance Seat (Item 23)
conflicts.summary: Council and transit staff examined diverging priorities between overall survey respondents favoring commuter rail and POC/daily riders prioritizing late-night/Sunday bus service, alongside City governance representation and light-rail accountability.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize immediate frequency, late-night/weekend reliability, and a full City voting seat on the Staff Working Group alongside pursuing regional rail without over-promising.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson emphasized that transit-dependent riders and POC respondents ranked evening/Sunday bus improvements far higher than commuter rail.

Steve Schewel argued Durham owns the GoDurham bus system and contributes substantial property taxes, making a voting City seat on the Staff Working Group essential, while Mark-Anthony Middleton called for transparent accounting of past light-rail expenditures.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain focus on dual local-and-regional investments including Option C (commuter rail) connectivity, especially near permanently subsidized downtown affordable housing.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero argued Durham will fail unless it delivers both better local bus service and a regional transit system (Options A and C combined).

Schewel also noted Option C nearly doubles 45-minute job accessibility from subsidized downtown housing at 519 E. Main St., Willard St., and DHA sites, whereas Oxford Manor remains an accessibility outlier under all plans.
conflicts.resolution: Informational / Staff directed to bring recommended final transit plan and revised interlocal governance agreement in January 2022

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Timing, Tiering, and Public Input for City Council Living-Wage Compensation Increases
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to raise Council salaries to a ~$35,000 living wage starting in 2022 or defer any raise until after public engagement and the 2021 election.
conflicts.side_a_position: Move forward promptly toward a ~$35,000 living-wage base in 2022 so working-class candidates and sitting members without independent wealth can afford to serve.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon and Javiera Caballero argued that low part-time stipends exclude lower-income residents from running or remaining on Council and urged an earlier 2022 effective date rather than waiting until 2024.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not enact unvetted mid-budget raises or tiered salaries before the municipal election; defer to public input and a post-election November vote.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece, Steve Schewel, and Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed voting themselves a mid-budget raise without prior public budget engagement, and Middleton also objected to tiered salary levels.
conflicts.resolution: By consensus (03:10:40-03:14:51), Council set aside roughly $80,000 in 'appropriations not authorized' in the FY22 budget to preserve funding capacity for a November 2021 vote after public engagement.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Rosewalk II Traffic & Intersection Safety vs. Central Infill Multifamily Housing
conflicts.summary: Neighbors of Trinity Park and Northgate Park argued that Rosewalk II's 310 apartments would exacerbate crashes at N. Duke St and W. Club Blvd and cut-through speeding while sidestepping a Traffic Impact Analysis under the 149-trip cap, whereas council members prioritized centrally located rental supply once additional proffers were added.
conflicts.side_a_position: Delay or require signal/geometric fixes and fuller neighborhood traffic mitigation before approving 310 apartments.
side_a_arguments: Residents reported repeated severe collisions and bus-passenger hazards at W. Club Blvd and N. Duke St.
Neighbors criticized capping trips below 149 to avoid a TIA and argued the driveway should be offset from Woodland Dr.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the 310-unit RU-M(D) rezoning based on central infill location, 35% lower projected rents than downtown, and new traffic/school proffers.
side_b_arguments: Lower land cost (~80% below downtown) and surface parking allow relatively moderate rents near Duke University and I-85.
Applicant committed $30,000 toward a neighborhood traffic circle and $20,500 for DPS students.
conflicts.resolution: Following the applicant's additional traffic-circle and school proffers and transportation staff review, Council unanimously passed the rezoning 7-0 while noting ongoing coordination with NCDOT.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Racial & Economic Equity of Special Assessments for Basic Water and Road Paving on Ardmore Drive
conflicts.summary: While voting unanimously to approve residents' $1.8M self-assessed petition so Ardmore Drive families receive clean water and fire protection immediately, council members criticized a city system that forces longtime Black working-class homeowners to pay steep assessments to skip a multi-year unpaved-road queue.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the resident petition now to end well contamination while condemning special assessments for basic municipal infrastructure.
side_a_arguments: Forcing residents annexed decades ago with bacteria-contaminated wells and no hydrants to pay ~$1.8M across 13-14 properties to jump ahead 4-5 years reflects systemic inequity.
Council urged reforming how Durham funds unpaved roads and water extensions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Note the statutory structure under which petitioned 100%-assessed improvements accelerate capital queue priority under existing policy.
side_b_arguments: Staff and Mayor Schewel noted the $1.8M estimate (~$1.2M paving, ~$600k water lines/laterals) relies on petitioner signatures to advance 4-5 years ahead of standard city-funded scheduling.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 7-0 on all three Ardmore Drive assessment motions so residents could receive water, fire service, and paving, while calling for future funding reforms.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Scope of Tenants' Bill of Rights Under State Preemption vs. Municipal Enforcement Resources
conflicts.summary: During the Item 9 Tenants' Bill of Rights discussion, Bull City Tenants United organizers and some council members pushed to adopt strong local anti-rent-collection and inspection ordinances modeled on Charlotte's code, while the City Attorney warned of NC state statutory preemption and council members debated how far Durham could push legal boundaries without risking invalidation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Push legal boundaries—mirroring Charlotte's minimum-housing rent prohibition and expanding after-hours inspections, translation, Ban-the-Box, and enforcement funding.
side_a_arguments: Tenants live in dangerous slum conditions and face landlords who ignore repairs or send maintenance staff as biased interpreters.
Charlotte's provision provides practical leverage for tenants seeking treble damages or warranty-of-habitability relief even without direct city prosecution.
conflicts.side_b_position: Focus on legally defensible city investments—free inspection access, language translation, eviction legal aid, and non-discrimination ordinances—while respecting NC statutory preemption.
side_b_arguments: North Carolina preemption and NCGS 42-44 prohibit cities from authorizing unilateral tenant rent withholding or escrow outside court orders, and Charlotte does not enforce its clause.
Municipal funding for legal defense and expanded code enforcement delivers immediate tangible tenant relief.
conflicts.resolution: Council directed the City Manager to assess staffing/funding for inspection access, interpretation, and landlord registration (items 1, 2, 4, 13), directed the City Attorney to review non-discrimination/Ban-the-Box/SOI options (items 3, 6, 11), and tasked DeDreana Freeman with drafting a symbolic resolution (item 8) for January 2022.

conflicts.meeting_title: Joint City-County Meeting Oct 12, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Legality, Business Impact, and Preemption Risk of Proposed 10-Cent Single-Use Bag Fee
conflicts.summary: Committee members and stakeholders debated whether Durham City and County have statutory authority to enact a 10-cent carryout bag fee framed as a stormwater utility mitigation measure without triggering litigation or state legislative retaliation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Pursue a local 10-cent single-use bag fee using stormwater/solid-waste regulatory authority to cut plastic pollution and litter-cleanup costs.
side_a_arguments: Duke Environmental Law Clinic presented legal analysis distinguishing a targeted mitigation fee tied to stormwater/waste impacts from prohibited general sales taxes.
Environmental advocates and Mayor Schewel noted voluntary outreach has failed to curb bag litter and pointed to other jurisdictions' sharp reductions after bag fees.
conflicts.side_b_position: Question statutory authority under North Carolina preemption rules and warn against retail compliance burdens and General Assembly retaliation.
side_b_arguments: NC Retail Merchants Association argued NCGS 160A-215.1 bars local taxes on retail sales and said small and grocery retailers oppose mandated bag-fee administration.
DeDreana Freeman warned that testing state preemption boundaries with a bag fee could provoke the General Assembly into restricting Durham's existing local stormwater utility fee.
conflicts.resolution: Informational / Requested formal legal review from the City Attorney and County Attorney before advancing an ordinance

conflicts.meeting_title: Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - October 6, 2021
conflicts.issue: Premature Application of Draft Southeast Durham Plan Policies & Comprehensive Plan Engagement
conflicts.summary: During the Comprehensive Plan update, Mark-Anthony Middleton raised strong concern that City Council colleagues were already citing the un-adopted draft Southeast Focus Area Plan against rezoning applications (such as Courtyards at Doc Nichols) before JCCPC review or adoption, alongside debate over how Planning engages local builders and residents.
conflicts.side_a_position: Do not apply un-adopted draft Southeast Durham Focus Area Plan maps to defeat current zoning cases, and provide more direct staff engagement channels for residents.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton noted developers and Council members lacked official clarity because the Southeast Focus Area Plan remained an un-adopted draft with open policy questions.
Middleton urged making Planning staff more directly accessible to citizens intimidated by technical mapping jargon.
conflicts.side_b_position: Use the draft place-type framework iteratively across fall community workshops and engage local infill practitioners before formal adoption.
side_b_arguments: Staff and Chair Jacobs clarified the Southeast Focus Area work was intended as an iterative testing lab rather than an adopted plan.
Javiera Caballero and Pierce Freelon emphasized incorporating local small-scale builders, architects, and multi-channel neighborhood workshops into refining the place types.
conflicts.resolution: Informational / Guidance provided to Planning staff ahead of fall workshops and November follow-up

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Premise and Efficacy of Municipal Corporate Incentives (Item 46 CARsgen Therapeutics)
conflicts.summary: While Council approved the $256,000 CARsgen Therapeutics incentive, members clashed philosophically over the 'but-for' constitutional fiction behind local corporate cash incentives versus net tax-revenue math.
conflicts.side_a_position: Vote Aye only under deep protest because municipal bidding wars force Durham into logically flawed cash giveaways to multi-billion-dollar firms.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:55:54, 04:00:19) argued a newly Hong Kong-listed company valued over $2B clearly did not need $256,000 from Durham 'but for' the grant to locate here, urging federal/state reform while voting yes to avoid losing jobs to competing states.
Jillian Johnson (03:57:50) concurred with Reece's protest.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support economic development incentives as pragmatic capital-leveraging investments yielding positive net property-tax returns and local jobs.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:58:10, 04:01:57) rejected characterizing incentives as morally questionable, noted finance projections showed tax revenues exceeding the $256,000 payout within three years, and urged coupling incentives with vocational training for Durham residents without college degrees (echoing Donald Hughes).
conflicts.resolution: Council approved the $256,000 incentive agreement.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 23, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: GoDurham Bus Operator Assaults and Unintended Consequences of Fare-Free Transit
conflicts.summary: Following GoDurham operator testimony on assaults and gunfire threats, members and public speakers differed sharply on whether fare-free transit contributed to onboard disorder.
conflicts.side_a_position: Affirm free transit while noting that zero-fare policy increased individuals riding with nowhere to go, creating more opportunities for conflict.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson emphasized fare-free buses remain a fabulous policy choice that must continue, while noting one unintended consequence reported in driver meetings was more people hanging out on buses.
Drivers cited mask-mandate enforcement conflicts alongside loss of prior private security at Durham Station.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject linking zero-fare transit access to criminal violence or assaults against drivers.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton stressed that fare price points do not deter violence and warned against any narrative stigmatizing low-income Black and brown transit riders.
Speaker Donald Hughes called linking free bus expansion to driver assaults 'appalling' and unsupported by data.
conflicts.resolution: Informational / Staff directed to pursue bus barriers, DPD coordination, and de-escalation training

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham Planning Commission & City Council Meeting 9/14/21 at 4 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Interim Legal Weight and Binding Language of Draft Southeast Focus Area Policies
conflicts.summary: Council members, Planning Commissioners, and legal/planning staff differed over how forcefully the unadopted Southeast Focus Area draft recommendations should be worded and applied to pending rezonings before formal Comprehensive Plan adoption in late 2022.
conflicts.side_a_position: Treat draft policies cautiously as non-binding advisory guidance and avoid legally unenforceable 'shall' mandates or density caps that risk court reversal.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (00:27:38, 01:11:48) cautioned against promising residents binding affordability AMI limits, traffic rules, or tree-preservation mandates that North Carolina law and existing UDO/Comprehensive Plan standards cannot sustain on judicial review.

Planning Director Sara Young (00:31:28) and Deputy City Attorney Don O'Toole (01:13:45) explained that the draft recommendations are not yet adopted policy and therefore carry limited legal weight compared to adopted plans and UDO rules.
conflicts.side_b_position: Apply the draft Southeast Focus Area map and 24 policies as strong interim guidance and strengthen policy language from 'should' toward enforceable expectations.
side_b_arguments: Planning Commissioners Baker, Durkin, and Amendolia argued that advisory 'should' phrasing invites developers to ignore community feedback and urged clearer commitments around density, affordability, and tree protection.

Mayor Steve Schewel (01:17:07) stated he would not take the draft recommendations with 'a grain of salt' and would treat them as significant interim guidance reflecting extensive Planning Commission and staff work.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; staff committed to refining the 24 draft policies for future public review and Comprehensive Plan integration while legal counsel advised keeping interim project reviews grounded in adopted ordinances.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 9, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 911 Alternate Routing Termination and Call-Center Response Adequacy
conflicts.summary: Following staff's presentation showing 28 FTE vacancies and sub-target 911 answer speeds in July 2021, council members criticized terminating Raleigh mutual-aid backup routing and questioned emergency response safety.
conflicts.side_a_position: Management decisions ending mutual-aid overflow routing to Raleigh and acute dispatcher shortages are compromising urgent resident safety and require immediate corrective remedies.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (04:15:40, 04:28:33) criticized the ending of mutual-aid routing with Raleigh and questioned whether residents in critical danger are waiting unacceptably long.

DeDreana Freeman (04:23:09) cited a four-minute wait during a Main Street shooting call she experienced and proposed a resolution classifying 911 telecommunicators as First Responders to bolster pay and retention.
conflicts.side_b_position: Raleigh's center faced parallel staffing/routing constraints, and Durham is addressing record July call volume (27,009 calls) through active hiring classes and compensation steps.
side_b_arguments: Director Randy Beaman and Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson explained operational factors behind the mutual-aid pause, noted a hiring pipeline underway, and cautioned that August metrics would likely mirror July's backlog.
conflicts.resolution: Informational report; no formal vote was taken while staff continued recruitment and Council flagged First Responder classification for potential follow-up.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: On-Street Parking Loss vs. Curbside Activation in Permanent Outdoor Seating Ordinance (Item 7)
conflicts.summary: Public comment and Council staff Q&A highlighted tension between downtown street-dining permits using metered parking spaces and off-corridor neighborhood businesses facing spill-over parking deficits.
conflicts.side_a_position: Make outdoor dining permanent citywide up to 50% of interior capacity while charging meter fees for occupied spaces and conducting curbside management review.
side_a_arguments: Outdoor dining kept locally owned downtown restaurants alive during COVID-19 and activates public streets.
Requiring restaurants to pay the meter rate avoids subsidizing parking loss, and the ordinance expands availability citywide alongside design templates.
conflicts.side_b_position: Address severe parking deficits in Central Park / Old North Durham and avoid effectively subsidizing downtown corridor businesses that convert public spaces.
side_b_arguments: Accordion Club owner Scott Ritchie testified that Geer Street businesses already suffer from overflow event parking deficits and lack sidewalks/street space to benefit equally from street-cafe permits.
Sidewalk cafes adjacent to businesses are reasonable, whereas claiming on-street parking spaces reduces affordable evening parking supply.
conflicts.resolution: Placed on Consent Agenda with transportation staff committing to curbside management coordination and neighbor notification review

meetings.title: Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - December 1, 2021
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by County Commissioner Wendy Jacobs with City Council representatives Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece, and Javiera Caballero present alongside Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and Planning Commissioner Austin Amendolia, the Joint City-County Planning Committee voted 6-0 to excuse Commissioner Brenda Howerton and approve the October 6, 2021 minutes. Planning staff presented the Comprehensive Plan Draft Place Type Map and engagement rollout, highlighting Urban Growth Boundary pullbacks near Falls Lake and 15-minute community concepts, and walked through Omnibus 17 UDO Text Amendments. Members directed staff to explore full parking-minimum elimination for existing building change-of-use and height/density incentives for solar and green buildings, while also reviewing Expanding Housing Choice Q3 2021 permit trends (194 permits since October 2019), Census data delays, and scheduling joint annual commission reports.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 18, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Opening the final work session chaired by retiring Mayor Steve Schewel, council members, City Manager Wanda Page, City Attorney Kim Rehberg, and City Clerk Diana Schreiber delivered farewell tributes before Council approved six unanimous 7-0 motions. Under suspended rules requested by the administration to expedite eviction prevention, Council approved two Emergency Rental Assistance (ERA2) contracts with Legal Aid of North Carolina and Benevate Inc. (Neighborly Software), while speakers raised concerns about landlords refusing ERA funds and Zoom chat deactivation. Council also reviewed pulled items—including Durham Athletic Park's 9th amendment, the $416,350 Built2Last Innovations Lab MOU, and $4M in standby storm-debris contracts—and received the Affordable Housing Implementation Committee's inaugural 6-month report and the FY2022 Q1 Financial Report highlighting fare-free transit and parking revenue shortfalls.

agenda_items.title: Farewell Tributes to Retiring Mayor Steve Schewel and Hillside High Shout-Out
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Colleagues Charlie Reece, Jillian Johnson, Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Javiera Caballero—followed by City Manager Wanda Page, City Attorney Kim Rehberg, and City Clerk Diana Schreiber—paid tribute to Mayor Steve Schewel at his final work session. Middleton also recognized Hillside High School students and theater director Wendell Tabb's 'State of Urgency' production.

agenda_items.title: Priority Item Adjustments and Immediate Approval of ERA2 Rental Assistance Contracts (Legal Aid & Benevate)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page requested suspending rules for immediate action on Items 4 and 5 and noted minor updates to Items 13 and 18, which Council approved 7-0. After public comment including Jacqueline Wagstaff questioning Zoom chat removal and landlord refusals of ERA funds, Council suspended the rules and unanimously approved Item 4 (Legal Aid NC eviction defense/ERA2 grant contract) and Item 5 (Benevate/Neighborly Software ERA2 SaaS contract) 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Items: Durham Athletic Park, Built2Last Innovations Lab MOU, and FEMA Debris Contracts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Schewel and Reece discussed long-term community stewardship and turf/event options for Durham Athletic Park (Item 10) following Durham Central Park's letter. Middleton and Stella Adams questioned startup governance and funding structure on the $416,350 Built2Last Innovations Lab MOU (Item 13) with Deputy City Manager Keith Chadwell, while Johnson and Schewel examined FEMA standby thresholds and minority/women employment on DRC Emergency Services ($3M, Item 15) and Tetra Tech ($1M, Item 16).

agenda_items.title: Affordable Housing Implementation Committee Inaugural 6-Month Report (Forever Home Durham)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and committee co-chairs Tiffany Elder and Diane Catotti presented the committee's first semi-annual report tracking Forever Home Durham bond investments amid 25% annual home-price escalation (median ~$397k) and 20% pandemic rent hikes. Presentations highlighted Willard Street (82 units), Laurel Oaks (34 preserved units), UMCNC's $130M MWBE capacity target, and how pre-July 2019 baseline rules count projects.

agenda_items.title: FY2022 Q1 Financial Report and Settling the December 6 Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance/Budget staff including Christina Riordan presented the FY2022 Q1 financial report, detailing a $2.7M Transit Fund shortfall under fare-free service and a $2.5M fund balance draw in the Parking Fund ahead of upcoming rate/fee discussions. Council then voted 7-0 to settle the December 6 agenda (Consent 1-3, 6-16; GBA Public Hearings 18-19) before Mayor Schewel struck the gavel for his final adjournment.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Returning to City Hall chambers for Durham's first hybrid regular meeting, Council proclaimed David Price Day and Veterans Day, recognized 911 dispatcher Dwayne McIntyre, and hosted nearly 90 minutes of community tributes honoring retiring Council Member Pierce Freelon and Mayor Steve Schewel. Council unanimously passed the Consent Agenda 7-0 (including five Crane/Elizabeth/Eva/Gurley/Marne affordable-housing land conveyances) and adopted UDO Text Amendment TC2104 (tenant notification and permit updates) 7-0. After an extended public hearing over traffic, signalization, and school capacity, Council approved the 310-apartment Rosewalk II rezoning at West Club Blvd and North Duke St 7-0 after applicants proffered $30,000 for a traffic circle and $20,500 for DPS students, and then unanimously voted 7-0 across three motions to order $1.8M in petitioned Ardmore Drive ribbon paving and water/sewer lines while criticizing special-assessment inequity.

agenda_items.title: David Price Day, Veterans Day, 911 Dispatcher Tribute, and Farewells to Freelon & Schewel
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In Durham's first hybrid in-person meeting since the pandemic, Council presented proclamations for Congressman David Price Day and Veterans Day and honored 911 dispatcher Dwayne McIntyre. disagreements.issue: Scope of Tenants' Bill of Rights Under State Preemption vs. Municipal Enforcement Resources
disagreements.summary: During the Item 9 Tenants' Bill of Rights discussion, Bull City Tenants United organizers and some council members pushed to adopt strong local anti-rent-collection and inspection ordinances modeled on Charlotte's code, while the City Attorney warned of NC state statutory preemption and council members debated how far Durham could push legal boundaries without risking invalidation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Push legal boundaries—mirroring Charlotte's minimum-housing rent prohibition and expanding after-hours inspections, translation, Ban-the-Box, and enforcement funding.
side_a_arguments: Tenants live in dangerous slum conditions and face landlords who ignore repairs or send maintenance staff as biased interpreters.

disagreements.side_b_position: Focus on legally defensible city investments—free inspection access, language translation, eviction legal aid, and non-discrimination ordinances—while respecting NC statutory preemption.
side_b_arguments: North Carolina preemption and NCGS 42-44 prohibit cities from authorizing unilateral tenant rent withholding or escrow outside court orders, and Charlotte does not enforce its clause.
Municipal funding for legal defense and expanded code enforcement delivers immediate tangible tenant relief.
disagreements.resolution: Council directed the City Manager to assess staffing/funding for inspection access, interpretation, and landlord registration (items 1, 2, 4, 13), directed the City Attorney to review non-discrimination/Ban-the-Box/SOI options (items 3, 6, 11), and tasked DeDreana Freeman with drafting a symbolic resolution (item 8) for January 2022.

meetings.executive_summary: Convening shortly after an extended closed session with Charlie Reece on an excused absence, the October 7, 2021 Work Session saw Council suspend the rules (6-0) to immediately adopt the grant budget ordinance and MOU with StepUp Durham and the Reinvent Stockton Foundation for Project Excel, Durham's guaranteed income pilot (6-0). During Citizen Matters and pulled Item 9, residents Larisa Seibel, gunshot-injury victim Sanden Nelson, and Donald Hughes underscored acute eviction and ERAP delays as Community Development Director Reginald Johnson explained Durham County DSS could no longer administer the city's $6.6 million ERAP 2 tranche, forcing the city to search urgently for an external administrator alongside approving $1.8 million in COVID ESG homelessness and shelter contracts. Council also heard Accordion Club owner Scott Ritchie's parking-loss objections on the permanent Outdoor Seating Ordinance (Item 7), reviewed the 20-year $88 million Carbon Neutrality and Renewable Energy Action Plan (Item 18) and Green Source Advantage solar filing (Item 19), and debated commuter rail versus bus-first equity trade-offs in Phase 2 Durham County Transit Plan survey findings before setting the October 18 agenda (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Project Excel Announcements, and City Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order at 1:05 PM after closed session with six members present and Charlie Reece on an excused absence; DeDreana Freeman did not respond during initial roll call and the first priority vote but joined before Item 5. Mark-Anthony Middleton praised StepUp Durham's fundraising for the Project Excel guaranteed income pilot, and Council approved City Manager Wanda Page's priority additions—including urgent action on Item 5 and adding Item 26 (Walltown Longtime Homeowner Grant expansion)—by a 5-0 vote.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-0 (Freeman absent for roll call; Reece excused)

agenda_items.title: Project Excel Guaranteed Income MOU (StepUp Durham & Reinvent Stockton Foundation) and Grant Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: To meet an October/November 1 execution deadline, City Manager Wanda Page asked Council to suspend rules and adopt the Project Excel guaranteed income grant budget ordinance and MOU with StepUp Durham and the Reinvent Stockton Foundation. With DeDreana Freeman present, Council suspended the rules 6-0 and adopted the ordinance and MOU 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Urgent Eviction Prevention & ERAP 2 Access Appeals (Seibel, Nelson, Hughes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Larisa Seibel and McDougald Terrace shooting victim Sanden Nelson urged Council to rapidly reopen the city's Emergency Rental Assistance Program after County ERAP closed and DSS denied Nelson assistance while recovering from a chest wound. Later at 00:43:26, Donald Hughes pressed Council to fund immediate emergency rental relief ahead of considering Council salary increases.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item: Permanent Citywide Outdoor Seating Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff (Mr. Dubrinsky) and Transportation Director Sean Egan reviewed downtown restaurant feedback (including Elizabeth Turnbull's suggestion of pre-approved templates) and clarified the corrected 50% interior cap and citywide scope. Downtown Durham Inc.'s Nicole Thompson backed permanent outdoor dining, whereas Accordion Club owner Scott Ritchie objected that losing on-street downtown parking harms bars/restaurants outside the downtown loop and amounts to a city subsidy.

agenda_items.title: ERAP 2 ($6.6M) Administrator Search and Interlocking $1.8M ESG-CV Homelessness Contracts (Items 9-13)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson explained that Durham County DSS declined to administer the city's $6.6 million ERAP 2 allocation due to capacity overload, leaving the city searching for scarce third-party vendors (including exploring Legal Aid partnerships) while City Manager Wanda Page joined the recruitment effort. Homeless System Manager Colin Davis then walked through how five interlocking ESG-CV contracts totaling $1.8 million (Families Moving Forward, Open Table Ministry, Project Access, Urban Ministries, and Volunteers of America) fund winter shelter, street homelessness prevention, and Carolina Duke Inn supportive services alongside County FEMA funds.

agenda_items.title: Quaker Creek Solar Farm & Duke Energy Green Source Advantage Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services Division Manager Summer Alston and Duke Energy Green Source Advantage Manager Wendy Flener briefed Council on an urgent September 17 Utilities Commission filing adjusting interconnection rules ahead of the October 31 program deadline. Both expressed optimism that Durham's 34.9 MW solar application with Quaker Creek Solar Farm will qualify, with August 2022 UNC/military unused capacity as a backup.

agenda_items.title: City of Durham Carbon Neutrality and Renewable Energy Action Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Summer Alston and GDS Associates Managing Director Angela Strickland presented Durham's 30-year Carbon Neutrality and Renewable Energy Action Plan targeting 50% GHG reduction and 80% renewables by 2030, carbon neutrality by 2040, and 100% renewable energy by 2050 via energy efficiency (12%), on-site/Green Source Advantage solar (44%), and fleet/transit electrification (44%) requiring ~$88 million in capital over 20 years offset by lifecycle savings. Council praised the concrete plan while urging minimal reliance on carbon offsets and swift EV bus/charging buildout.

agenda_items.title: Durham County Transit Plan Phase 2 Outreach Summary & Governance Study
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham County Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and DCHC MPO Planning Manager Aaron Cain presented Phase 2 engagement results from 2,300+ residents comparing Bus Improvements (Option A), Bus Rapid Transit (Option B), and Commuter Rail (Option C), showing daily riders and respondents of color prioritized late-night/Sunday bus frequency over rail. Mayor Schewel reiterated that the City must hold a full voting seat on the transit Staff Working Group, Mark-Anthony Middleton called for an accessible public accounting of past light-rail expenditures to rebuild trust, and Javiera Caballero urged doing both local bus improvements and regional transit.

agenda_items.title: Racial Equity Commission Nominations and Setting October 18 Council Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council confirmed consensus Racial Equity Commission nominations—Theodore Reuter (At-Large), Derrick S. Rhodes (Ward 1), Taylor Walker (Youth, pending city-residency verification), Tarik Woods (Ward 2 via vote switches), and Nisha Williams (Ward 3 via vote switches)—while re-advertising one At-Large seat. City Manager Wanda Page set the October 18 Consent Agenda (Items 1-4, 6-22, and 26) and GBA Public Hearings (Items 24-25), which Council approved 6-0 before adjourning at 4:06 PM.

votes.discussion_detail: Accepted the Manager's priority additions (requesting rule suspension on Item 5 Project Excel MOU, updating Item 13 attachment, noting Item 18 presentation, and adding supplemental Item 26 Walltown Longtime Homeowner Grant expansion). votes.notes: Charlie Reece had an excused absence.

votes.discussion_detail: Set the October 18 Regular Meeting agenda with Items 1-4, 6-22, and 26 on Consent and Items 24-25 on General Business Agenda Public Hearings.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: On-Street Parking Loss vs. Curbside Activation in Permanent Outdoor Seating Ordinance (Item 7)
disagreements.summary: Public comment and Council staff Q&A highlighted tension between downtown street-dining permits using metered parking spaces and off-corridor neighborhood businesses facing spill-over parking deficits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Make outdoor dining permanent citywide up to 50% of interior capacity while charging meter fees for occupied spaces and conducting curbside management review.
side_a_arguments: Outdoor dining kept locally owned downtown restaurants alive during COVID-19 and activates public streets.
Requiring restaurants to pay the meter rate avoids subsidizing parking loss, and the ordinance expands availability citywide alongside design templates.
disagreements.side_b_position: Address severe parking deficits in Central Park / Old North Durham and avoid effectively subsidizing downtown corridor businesses that convert public spaces.
side_b_arguments: Accordion Club owner Scott Ritchie testified that Geer Street businesses already suffer from overflow event parking deficits and lack sidewalks/street space to benefit equally from street-cafe permits.
Sidewalk cafes adjacent to businesses are reasonable, whereas claiming on-street parking spaces reduces affordable evening parking supply.
disagreements.resolution: Placed on Consent Agenda with transportation staff committing to curbside management coordination and neighbor notification review

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Durham County Transit Plan Priorities: Bus Service Equity, Commuter Rail Costs, and City Governance Seat (Item 23)
disagreements.summary: Council and transit staff examined diverging priorities between overall survey respondents favoring commuter rail and POC/daily riders prioritizing late-night/Sunday bus service, alongside City governance representation and light-rail accountability.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prioritize immediate frequency, late-night/weekend reliability, and a full City voting seat on the Staff Working Group alongside pursuing regional rail without over-promising.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson emphasized that transit-dependent riders and POC respondents ranked evening/Sunday bus improvements far higher than commuter rail.

Steve Schewel argued Durham owns the GoDurham bus system and contributes substantial property taxes, making a voting City seat on the Staff Working Group essential, while Mark-Anthony Middleton called for transparent accounting of past light-rail expenditures.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain focus on dual local-and-regional investments including Option C (commuter rail) connectivity, especially near permanently subsidized downtown affordable housing.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero argued Durham will fail unless it delivers both better local bus service and a regional transit system (Options A and C combined).

Schewel also noted Option C nearly doubles 45-minute job accessibility from subsidized downtown housing at 519 E. Main St., Willard St., and DHA sites, whereas Oxford Manor remains an accessibility outlier under all plans.
disagreements.resolution: Informational / Staff directed to bring recommended final transit plan and revised interlocal governance agreement in January 2022

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: With Charlie Reece on an excused absence, the six-member City Council deadlocked 3-3 on Item 16, defeating Epcon Communities' 133-home Courtyards at Doc Nichols annexation and rezoning (Ayes: Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton; Nays: Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero) over tensions between accessible senior housing and solar conduit proffers versus low 1.8 units/acre density, $500k+ pricing, stream crossings, and the Planning Commission's 0-12 denial. Earlier, Council unanimously approved the Consent Agenda (6-0, excluding Items 10 and 19). On pulled items, Council passed the $6,000 Poet Laureate Pilot Program (Item 10, 6-0), approved a CVS Health weekly COVID-19 employee testing contract up to $839,440 (Item 19, two 6-0 votes, with DeDreana Freeman voting 'very hesitantly aye' over the $70/month health insurance wellness surcharge), and adopted the Resolution in Support of Safe and Healthy Housing (Item 21, 6-0).

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Proclamations, and Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the meeting to order with six members present and Charlie Reece on an excused absence, reading proclamations including encouraging voter turnout for the next day's election. Council pulled Item 10 (Poet Laureate Pilot) and Item 19 (Weekly COVID-19 Testing LOA) for public speakers and approved the remaining Consent Agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Consolidated Annexation, Zoning Map Change, and FLUM Amendment — Courtyards at Doc Nichols
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a lengthy public hearing on Epcon Communities' proposal to annex 75 acres on Doc Nichols Road and build 133 single-story accessible homes (1.8 units/acre) featuring a $120,000 affordable housing contribution, 33% tree preservation, and Durham's first solar-conduit proffer despite a 0-12 Planning Commission recommendation for denial. Following neighborhood opposition over traffic and stream impacts alongside union/equity support for aging-in-place housing, Council deadlocked 3-3, causing the project to fail.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item: City of Durham Poet Laureate Pilot Program ($6,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After hearing public comment regarding the $6,000 pilot program funding and selection structure recommended by the Durham Cultural Advisory Board, Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson moved and Pierce Freelon seconded approval of the Poet Laureate pilot. Council passed the item unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item: Weekly COVID-19 Employee Testing Letter of Agreement with CVS Health ($839,440 Cap)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council heard from staff and public comment on the 12-week on-site CVS Health weekly COVID-19 testing contract paired with Option 3's $70/month 2022 wellness insurance surcharge for unvaccinated employees. DeDreana Freeman voiced lingering reservations about coercion and employee impact—casting a 'very hesitantly aye' vote—as Council passed both motions authorizing the LOA up to $839,440 and allowing minor contract negotiations within that cap.

agenda_items.title: Resolution in Support of Safe and Healthy Housing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council took up DeDreana Freeman's resolution affirming HUD healthy-home principles and city support for tenant protections against mold, lead, pests, carbon monoxide, and radon. Following one public speaker's comments, Council adopted the resolution 6-0 and adjourned at 9:13 PM.

meetings.title: Virtual Special Council Meeting Sept 30, 2021 (Live Stream)

Council also unanimously (7-0) granted Charlie Reece excused absences for the upcoming October 4 Regular Meeting and October 7 Work Session before adjourning at 10:14 AM.

agenda_items.title: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) $51.8M Allocation Process and Equity Scorecard

Pierce Freelon and DeDreana Freeman requested vetting scorecard weights with Black-led community organizations.

agenda_items.title: FY2020-21 Fourth Quarter Financial Report and Fund Balance Surplus
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget staff (John Allore) reported a $26.6 million General Fund positive variance—comprising $8.4 million in underspending and $18.2 million in stronger-than-projected revenues led by $14 million in sales taxes and $5 million in property taxes—pushing projected unrestricted fund balance to $67.8 million ($34.7M above the 16.7% policy floor). disagreements.issue: City Funding of Weekly COVID-19 Testing (Item 25 CVS Health Contract) vs. Vaccine Mandate or Employee-Paid Testing
disagreements.summary: Council divided sharply over City Manager Wanda Page's proposed $69,700/week CVS Health contract to fund weekly testing for unvaccinated employees out of the self-insured Health Insurance Fund, ultimately pulling the item before a formal vote.
disagreements.side_a_position: Do not spend taxpayer or shared employee Health Insurance Fund dollars to subsidize ongoing weekly testing for unvaccinated staff; move toward a vaccine mandate or higher health premiums/employee-paid testing.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel (01:14:19, 02:02:35) argued that paying nearly $70,000/week unfairly shifts costs onto taxpayers and vaccinated employees, urging either a vaccine mandate or requiring unvaccinated workers to pay for testing or higher premiums.
Charlie Reece (via email read at 02:08:53) opposed subsidizing weekly testing and favored a vaccine mandate with medical/religious exemptions and higher premiums for unvaccinated staff.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain a measured transition toward vaccination while addressing UE150 labor concerns, work-hours testing access, attrition risks, and EBO/diversity standards before imposing punitive penalties or mandates.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (01:19:41, 02:10:48), Jillian Johnson (01:47:01, 02:05:02), Javiera Caballero (01:28:16, 02:05:48), and Pierce Freelon (01:34:38, 02:06:55) questioned attrition impacts (with HR staff Anna Davis citing 3% at Houston Methodist and 2% at UVA), testing on work hours, UE150 union proposals, and delay options to examine premium recoupment or vaccine mandates.
Donald Hughes (01:43:41) urged Council not to waive Equal Business Opportunity diversity goals on the testing contract.
disagreements.resolution: By consensus (02:14:26-02:19:43), Item 25 was held off the regular meeting agenda, and City Manager Wanda Page agreed to cancel the October 18 testing start and return with data and revised options for a vaccine mandate or premium adjustments.

During the mid-meeting break at 02:15:31, Charlie Reece excused himself due to a family health issue, leaving six voting members for the final two items. Council then voted 5-1 (DeDreana Freeman dissenting) to annex 222 acres along Junction and Ferrell Roads (Item 19, over 1 million sq ft of industrial capacity by Scannell Properties) and adopted its companion Industrial Light translation zoning, before voting 6-0 to authorize a $150,000 economic development incentive for Nuvotronics Inc. tied to $39M-$50M capital investment and 113-150 jobs.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning — Courtyards at Southpoint 2 (7852 Herndon Rd & 1404 Fenwick Pkwy)

meetings.title: Budget Healing Event
meetings.executive_summary: On August 6, 2021, the City of Durham hosted Part 2 of its ARPA Budget Healing Series—co-facilitated by Budget Director Bertha Johnson, Leela Pedersen, Deputy City Manager Claudia Hager, Equity & Inclusion Director Sharon Williams, and NCCU professor Dr. Jim C. Harper II, with participation from Council members Javiera Caballero, Jillian Johnson, and Pierce Freelon. Presenters summarized over 300 community survey responses and 80 community funding proposals competing for Durham's $52 million city (and $62 million county) American Rescue Plan Act allocations, highlighting live Mentimeter prioritization polls topped by economic recovery, mental health, affordable housing, teacher pay, livable wages, and racial equity. Equity & Inclusion Director Sharon Williams introduced the Racial Equity Impact Assessment tool for evaluating ARPA proposals, followed by resident Q&A raising visually impaired website accessibility (Michelle Bush), application barriers for grassroots groups (Jesse Huddleston), and transition plans across the 2021 municipal election cycle addressed by Javiera Caballero before her closing remarks.

agenda_items.title: Introductions, Council Recognition, and ARPA Engagement Context
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Facilitator Leela Pedersen and NCCU's Dr. Jim C. Harper II welcomed residents alongside Council members Javiera Caballero, Jillian Johnson, and Pierce Freelon and Budget Director Bertha Johnson. Staff framed Part 2 of the Budget Healing series around community governance over $52 million in City ARPA funds alongside $62 million in County ARPA funds.

agenda_items.title: Review of 300+ Survey Responses, 80 Community Proposals, and Live Prioritization Polls
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Leela Pedersen and Bertha Johnson presented themes from over 300 community surveys and 80 submitted ARPA project ideas, followed by interactive Mentimeter ranking exercises with participants. Top resident priorities were Economic Impacts (overall category), Mental Health (public health), Affordable Housing (housing), Teacher Pay (education), Livable Wages (employment), and Racial Equity (evaluation criteria).

agenda_items.title: Racial Equity Impact Assessment Tool Presentation by Equity & Inclusion Director Sharon Williams
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Equity & Inclusion Director Sharon Williams walked through Durham's Racial Equity Impact Assessment (REIA) framework intended to score ARPA proposals against historical racial disparities, community co-creation, and unintended burdens. Staff noted how REIA scoring would feed into Council's upcoming fall ARPA evaluation rubric.

agenda_items.title: Community Questions on Accessibility, Grassroots Barriers, Election Transition, and Closing Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Participants questioned accessibility for visually impaired residents on city ARPA portals (Michelle Bush), criticized repetitive new application burdens rather than relying on prior task-force work (Jesse Huddleston), and asked how upcoming 2021 elections might impact ARPA decisions. Javiera Caballero explained Council continuity and upcoming fall allocation milestones at 01:09:21 before delivering closing remarks at 01:33:27.
