meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: In a nearly five-hour session concluding the 2020-21 fiscal year, Durham City Council unanimously adopted the FY2021-22 Budget and FY2022-27 CIP (7-0), alongside pulled Consent loans for Commerce Street Apartments and Elizabeth Street Apartments (7-0) and a GoTriangle transit improvements ILA prioritizing Braggtown bus stops (7-0). Council also unanimously adopted Comprehensive Plan Community Goals and Objectives (7-0), excused annexation for Bertha Gamble's 1518 Hamlin Road residence under a utility extension agreement (7-0), annexed and directly zoned two industrial projects on Lumley Road and Project Suite/1 Litho Way (7-0), and passed resolutions backing the American Jobs Plan and supporting the DPS Board against NC HB 324 (7-0). After extensive debate over the East Durham Open Space Plan, mass grading, distributed tree cover, and cemetery relocation at 1051 Olive Branch Road (Item 43), Council continued the public hearing to September 7, 2021. Council split 6-1 (Javiera Caballero dissenting) on a $10 million TEFRA bond resolution for private Duke School (Item 45), approved a $256,000 incentive for CARsgen Therapeutics (with Charlie Reece and Jillian Johnson voting aye under protest), and closed by directing staff to extend current Longtime Homeowner Grant applications through August 31 while returning in early August with a scoping plan for a gap-year citywide vs. targeted neighborhood tax-relief program.

agenda_items.title: Tribute to Alethea Bell, Proclamations, Council Announcements, and Consent Item 7 Referral
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened with a tribute to former HR Director Alethea Bell, followed by proclamations for Cleft and Craniofacial Awareness Month (student Kai Hale), Olympic Day (Marcus Manning & Hill Carrow), and Mayor's Monarch Pledge Day (Ashley Robbins). Council members celebrated the 35th anniversary of Durham's 1986 anti-discrimination proclamation and Juneteenth, discussed remote meeting rules and Morreene Road DHA plumbing issues, accepted priority items, and voted 7-0 to refer a third Workforce Development Board appointment back to committee before passing the unpulled Consent Agenda 7-0.

agenda_items.title: FY2021-22 Budget and FY2022-27 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Fayetteville Street Planning Group member Larry Hester urged 24-hour walking/bicycle patrols and corridor investment, while Donald Hughes urged doubling the Durham YouthWorks summer jobs budget and tracking public-engagement budget changes. Council adopted the FY2021-22 budget and FY2022-27 CIP 7-0; afterward, Denise Hester was heard under Zoom audio troubleshooting urging Fayetteville Street master-plan infrastructure funding, joined in remarks by DeDreana Freeman.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items: Commerce Street Apartments, Elizabeth Street Apartments, and Transit ILA
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman questioned income-tier allocations and funding sources on three pulled Consent items. DHA CEO Anthony Scott confirmed the shift from competitive 9% to non-competitive 4% LIHTC tax credits on Commerce Street kept 30%/60% AMI targets intact while bundling mixed-income and senior units (Item 12); Reginald Johnson confirmed Affordable Housing Bond backing for Elizabeth Street (Item 17); and Transportation Director Sean Egan committed to prioritizing Braggtown Route 9 stops with GoTriangle (Item 20).
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 7-0 each across three Roll Call votes

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Community Goals and Objectives Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Scott Whiteman presented the updated Comprehensive Plan Community Goals and Objectives incorporating Audubon Society biodiversity language from the June 15 joint hearing. After DeDreana Freeman requested clearer staff feedback loops for neighborhood groups such as the InterNeighborhood Council, Council adopted the resolution 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation / Utility Extension Alternative — Bertha Gamble Residence (1518 Hamlin Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Alexander Cahill explained that 1518 Hamlin Road is a 16.5-acre single-family home site whose septic is county-permitted but whose wells failed after construction began during COVID permitting delays, returning a revenue-negative fiscal impact. Representative Glenn White and homeowner Bertha Gamble explained their water hardship and agreed to Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson's request for a voluntary Affordable Housing Fund donation; Council adopted staff's alternative motion 7-0 excusing annexation under Code Sec. 70-129(9) while authorizing a landowner-funded water extension.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — Lumley Road Industrial (5605 & 5513 Lumley Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and H&S Venture Group (Wyatt Bone, Justin Parker) presented a 7.5-acre contiguous annexation and direct Industrial Light translation for a 75,000 sq ft industrial facility. After Charlie Reece and DeDreana Freeman questioned tenant displacement from two existing houses on site and Justin Parker confirmed the prior tenant had already moved out, Council approved annexation/UEA and UDO zoning translation 7-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 7-0 across two Roll Call votes

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning — 1051 Olive Branch Road (Continued to Sept. 7)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Danny Cultra and the Pulte Home Company LLC / Horvath Associates team (attorneys Matthews and Jamie Schwedler, engineer Tim Sivers, and Jamie Davis) presented a 79.478-acre annexation and PDR 3.700 rezoning for 284 units, which the Planning Commission opposed 1-11; former Council member Larissa Seibel spoke in opposition. Extended Council questioning challenged East Durham Open Space Plan compatibility, mass grading, peripheral tree save, highway-aligned road relocation of an on-site cemetery, and housing affordability impacts, prompting Council and applicant Tim Sivers to leave the public hearing open and continue Item 43 to September 7.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — Project Suite (1 Litho Way)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and applicant representative Justin Parker presented a 5.5-acre satellite-infill annexation and Industrial Light zoning translation for a 41,000 sq ft manufacturing addition next to an existing 100,000 sq ft facility. At City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg's request to separate the utility extension agreement onto its own motion, Council approved annexation, the A.L. Meyer LLC UEA, and UDO zoning in three unanimous 7-0 votes.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 7-0 across three Roll Call votes

agenda_items.title: TEFRA Revenue Bond Resolution ($10M Not-to-Exceed) for Duke School
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy Finance Director Emily Desiderio, bond counsel Jeff Paulie, and Duke School finance director Russell Rabinowitz sought statutory federal TEFRA approval for up to $10 million in Public Finance Authority bonds carrying no city debt obligation. Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned Duke School's $20,000-$23,000 tuition, 36% students of color, lack of free/reduced lunch or busing, and reliance on city emergency services before voting aye, while Javiera Caballero voted nay as the resolution passed 6-1.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with CARsgen Therapeutics Ltd. ($256,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Adria Graham Scott, Chamber's Brian Fox, Dr. Jia, and Donald Hughes spoke on a $256,000 performance-based city incentive paired with $1M County and $1.2M+ state JDIG awards for CARsgen Therapeutics' $97M phase-1 clinical manufacturing facility and 128 jobs allowing associate-degree hires. Charlie Reece and Jillian Johnson criticized the 'but-for' legal premise of corporate incentives for a $2B+ company while agreeing to vote yes under protest, Mark-Anthony Middleton defended positive fiscal math, and Council approved the agreement.

agenda_items.title: Resolutions Supporting the American Jobs Plan and Opposing NC House Bill 324
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Returning from a late-evening break, Council rapidly adopted two supplemental legislative resolutions by 7-0 roll-call votes: Item 49 endorsing the federal American Jobs Plan, and Item 50 supporting the Durham Public Schools Board of Education in opposing NC House Bill 324.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: 1051 Olive Branch Road Environmental Protections, Grave Relocation, and Suburban Housing Supply (Item 43)
disagreements.summary: Council held a prolonged debate over Pulte Home Company LLC's 284-unit annexation at 1051 Olive Branch Road, pitting housing-supply concerns against East Durham Open Space Plan incompatibility, mass grading, peripheral tree save, and relocation of an on-site cemetery, resulting in continuance to September 7.
disagreements.side_a_position: Continue the hearing to seek stronger tree preservation, environmental mitigation, and cemetery/community commitments without immediately killing needed housing stock.
side_a_arguments: Javiera Caballero (02:49:21) and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson (03:08:56) stressed Durham's worsening housing shortage while agreeing existing open questions justified a continuance.

Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:13:19) argued $230k-$300k housing expands supply for working-class firefighters, teachers, and officers while still expressing concern over the gravesite and the negligible 21%-to-22% tree-save increase.

Mayor Steve Schewel (03:04:54) backed increasing supply in Southeast Durham but warned he would vote no immediately given the 'not compatible with East Durham Open Space Plan' staff finding and environmental sensitivity.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose or demand deep substantive redesigns addressing far-flung Southeast Durham sprawl, cost-burden spillover, climate/mass-grading harm, and cemetery removal.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (02:57:53) questioned whether townhouses in far-east Durham near Morrisville actually curb gentrification in Braggtown or Walltown and argued annexation conferred no net benefit to Durham.

DeDreana Freeman (02:23:07, 03:10:27) highlighted cumulative impacts across nine area rezonings, carbon footprint without transit, nearby cost-burdened neighborhoods, and distress over moving a historic cemetery—noting she only supported a continuance if meaningful tree-save and stream-crossing changes returned.
disagreements.resolution: With applicant Tim Sivers' agreement (03:23:52), Council left the public hearing open and continued Item 43 to September 7, 2021.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Duke School $10M Tax-Exempt Revenue Bond Host-Approval Resolution (Item 45)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to pass the federal TEFRA resolution for private Duke School's revenue bonds, with Javiera Caballero voting Nay and Mark-Anthony Middleton raising equity concerns about private tuition and public-service reliance.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the routine ministerial TEFRA resolution because the City of Durham incurs zero debt, financial obligation, or taxpayer liability.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:41:30), Pierce Freelon (03:39:47), DeDreana Freeman (03:42:27), and Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:42:00) agreed that federal tax-law pass-through approval carries no city financial risk, though Middleton pressed Duke School officials on $20k-$23k tuition, lack of free/reduced lunch or busing, and reliance on city police/fire.
disagreements.side_b_position: Decline to lend City host-jurisdiction TEFRA approval to a private school revenue bond issuance.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero cast the sole Nay vote on roll call (03:43:18) without stating floor remarks.
disagreements.resolution: TEFRA resolution passed 6-1.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Premise and Efficacy of Municipal Corporate Incentives (Item 46 CARsgen Therapeutics)
disagreements.summary: While Council approved the $256,000 CARsgen Therapeutics incentive, members clashed philosophically over the 'but-for' constitutional fiction behind local corporate cash incentives versus net tax-revenue math.
disagreements.side_a_position: Vote Aye only under deep protest because municipal bidding wars force Durham into logically flawed cash giveaways to multi-billion-dollar firms.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:55:54, 04:00:19) argued a newly Hong Kong-listed company valued over $2B clearly did not need $256,000 from Durham 'but for' the grant to locate here, urging federal/state reform while voting yes to avoid losing jobs to competing states.
Jillian Johnson (03:57:50) concurred with Reece's protest.
disagreements.side_b_position: Support economic development incentives as pragmatic capital-leveraging investments yielding positive net property-tax returns and local jobs.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:58:10, 04:01:57) rejected characterizing incentives as morally questionable, noted finance projections showed tax revenues exceeding the $256,000 payout within three years, and urged coupling incentives with vocational training for Durham residents without college degrees (echoing Donald Hughes).
disagreements.resolution: Council approved the $256,000 incentive agreement.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Longtime Homeowner Grant Program Expansion: Citywide vs. Targeted Equity and Staff Capacity
disagreements.summary: Following Charlie Reece's proposal to hold applications open and rapidly craft a temporary citywide homeowner tax-relief program ahead of the joint City-County program, Council debated equity targeting, included neighborhoods (Braggtown, Merrick-Moore, Walltown), and Community Development staffing capacity.
disagreements.side_a_position: Create a temporary citywide property-tax relief program for the 2020-21 gap year to ensure all burdened longtime low-income homeowners qualify legally and equitably until the joint County program improves.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (04:11:36, 04:18:09, 04:32:16) argued citywide investments city-wide justify legal defensibility whereas ad-hoc neighborhood additions face legal hurdles cited by Assistant City Attorney Krista Kucera, offering to sunset the city program once the County raises AMI limits and benefit caps.
DeDreana Freeman (04:16:52, 04:27:11, 04:50:24) prioritized immediate gap-year relief so Braggtown, Merrick-Moore, and Walltown residents are not left out of 2019-2020 tax cycles.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep the 2019 cycle under current parameters through August 31 and avoid a rushed citywide expansion without staff capacity, cost modeling, and equity targeting.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (04:23:20, 04:41:41, 04:51:47) argued against blanket 'equality' floodgates in affluent areas in favor of targeted 'equity' investments (sidewalks, safety, targeted relief) in historically disinvested neighborhoods, citing Reginald Johnson's staffing constraints.

Jillian Johnson (04:28:51, 04:35:56), Pierce Freelon (04:45:52), and Steve Schewel (04:37:30, 04:48:50) respected staff capacity warnings (vacancies from retirement and medical leave) and supported letting the current program finish through Aug. 31 while directing staff to return in early August with a scoping and resource plan-to-make-a-plan.
disagreements.resolution: Council reached consensus thumbs-up (04:53:00-04:53:17) allowing staff to extend current applications administratively to August 31 and bring an assessment/scoping timeline for gap-year options to the first August work session.

meetings.executive_summary: At the June 10, 2021 City Council Work Session—where Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson called the meeting to order before Mayor Steve Schewel presided and later traded the gavel back to Johnson during Council salary and violence-prevention items—Council passed four unanimous 7-0 procedural roll-call votes (suspending rules for Citizens Advisory Committee corrections, appointing Shena M. disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Timing, Tiering, and Public Input for City Council Living-Wage Compensation Increases
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to raise Council salaries to a ~$35,000 living wage starting in 2022 or defer any raise until after public engagement and the 2021 election.
disagreements.side_a_position: Move forward promptly toward a ~$35,000 living-wage base in 2022 so working-class candidates and sitting members without independent wealth can afford to serve.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon and Javiera Caballero argued that low part-time stipends exclude lower-income residents from running or remaining on Council and urged an earlier 2022 effective date rather than waiting until 2024.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not enact unvetted mid-budget raises or tiered salaries before the municipal election; defer to public input and a post-election November vote.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece, Steve Schewel, and Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed voting themselves a mid-budget raise without prior public budget engagement, and Middleton also objected to tiered salary levels.
disagreements.resolution: By consensus (03:10:40-03:14:51), Council set aside roughly $80,000 in 'appropriations not authorized' in the FY22 budget to preserve funding capacity for a November 2021 vote after public engagement.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: 'We Are The Ones' Violence Prevention Funding Amount, Fund Source, and Scope (Mini-Grants vs. Mutual Aid/Centers)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 6-1 over how much extra money to allocate from fund balance—versus ARPA—and whether funding should be restricted strictly to mini-grants.
disagreements.side_a_position: Provide an extra $187,600 from fund balance to bring 'We Are The Ones' mini-grants to $250,000 total immediately in FY22.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Charlie Reece, and Mark-Anthony Middleton supported reaching $250,000 immediately to empower grassroots violence-prevention mini-grants rather than deferring to uncertain ARPA scoring.

Restricting the $250,000 allocation to mini-grants addressed concerns from Budget Director Bertha Johnson and Javiera Caballero regarding ARPA procurement and unvetted mutual-aid or center line items.
disagreements.side_b_position: Limit extra one-time fund-balance dollars to $100,000 rather than $187,600 and scrutinize program design before committing $250,000.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel favored adding $100,000 rather than $187,600 to reach $250,000 and cast the sole Nay vote when the $187,600 mini-grant motion was called.
disagreements.resolution: Council passed the $187,600 mini-grant allocation 6-1, with Steve Schewel dissenting.

meetings.title: Budget Healing Event June 8, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: On June 8, 2021, the City of Durham launched Part 1 of its Budget Healing Series focused on participatory community guidance for more than $51 million in City American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds (alongside more than $61 million for Durham County), hosted and opened by Council Member Pierce Freelon. Following an opening song ('Lift Every Voice and Sing' led by Nnenna Freelon), Pierce Freelon delivered a land acknowledgment and historical reflection on Hayti and urban renewal before announcing a quarterly Budget Healing cadence. NCCU professors Dr. Jim Harper II and Dr. Henry McKoy presented historical and racial economic-equity data, and Interim Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson outlined ARPA categories and the fall allocation timeline, before SpiritHouse co-director Nia Wilson led a healing meditation ahead of community breakout sessions.

agenda_items.title: Musical Opening, Land Acknowledgment, Urban Renewal Context, and Quarterly Series Launch
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Pierce Freelon welcomed residents to the first Budget Healing Event after Nnenna Freelon performed 'Lift Every Voice and Sing.' Freelon offered a land acknowledgment, spoke on the historical destruction of Hayti during urban renewal, and announced quarterly community budget healing sessions to democratize ARPA planning.

agenda_items.title: NCCU Presentations on Hayti History, Poverty Disparities, and Economic Inclusion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: FUSE fellow Leela Pedersen introduced NCCU history chair Dr. Jim Harper II and entrepreneurship director Dr. Henry McKoy. Dr. Harper reviewed Juneteenth and Black Wall Street history prior to urban renewal, while Dr. McKoy presented racial poverty and equity-index data showing stark disparities between White and Black/Hispanic households in Durham and urged community-led economic ecosystems.

agenda_items.title: Budget Office Briefing on Durham's ARPA Allocation, Timeline, and Equity Contacts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Deputy City Manager Bertha Johnson explained federal ARPA eligible uses and an allocation exceeding $51 million for the City (and $61 million for the County), alongside the April-September 2021 vetting and voting schedule. Johnson also recognized City and County equity leads Sharon Williams and Kweli Rashied-Henry and shared the online portal for resident proposals.

agenda_items.title: SpiritHouse Healing Meditation and Facilitated Community Breakout Dialogues
agenda_items.discussion_summary: SpiritHouse co-director Nia Wilson guided attendees through a grounding reflection confronting redlining and cultural suppression before participants moved into facilitated breakout dialogues on local budget priorities.
